paper_metadata.title: Efficient Hamiltonian Simulation for Solving Option Price Dynamics

summary: The paper proposes a gate-based digital quantum algorithm for Black-Scholes option pricing by mapping the PDE to a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and simulating it with QFT-assisted Hamiltonian simulation plus unitary dilation. The reported resource estimate is 9 logical qubits total, with expected post-selection success probability above 60%, but no hardware experiment or practical quantum advantage demonstration is provided.

experiments.description: Digital gate-based quantum algorithm for simulating Black-Scholes option-price dynamics via Hamiltonian simulation, using QFT-based diagonalization, unitary dilation with one ancilla qubit, and post-selection; evaluated on a discretized European put option instance with scalability up to 9 qubits in a fault-tolerant setting.

algorithm.variant: Black-Scholes Hamiltonian simulation with unitary dilation and post-selection; QFT-assisted simulation of diagonal momentum-space dynamics

hyperparameters.n_range: 1..8 for convergence plots; 8 for success-probability plots

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial condition loaded as the European put payoff state; duplicated by reflection to enforce periodic boundary conditions

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Position space discretized on Nx=2^n grid points; one qubit per spatial discretization bit, plus one ancilla for unitary dilation. Stock price mapped by S = exp(x).
problem_formulation.objective_function: Solve the Black-Scholes PDE by mapping it to a Schrödinger-like equation and simulating the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian evolution of the option price.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Periodic boundary conditions via duplication of the initial condition; non-Hermitian dynamics handled by unitary dilation and post-selection on ancilla |0⟩.

problem_instance.description: European put option pricing under the Black-Scholes model.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: Discretize x = log S on a finite interval; use payoff max(K-S,0) as terminal condition; duplicate initial condition for periodic boundary conditions.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Change variables S=exp(x); reverse time τ=T−t; discretize position and momentum with Nyquist-Shannon sampling and finite differences; use QFT to diagonalize the circulant momentum operator; duplicate the payoff state to mitigate edge effects.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compare numerical solution against analytical Black-Scholes solution; report convergence/error versus number of qubits; report post-selection success probability versus time to maturity, interest rate, number of points, and strike.

hardware.framework: Qiskit (implied by gate-based digital implementation references; not explicitly named in the provided text)

implementation_details.classical_solver: Analytical Black-Scholes solution for benchmarking; classical numerical comparison mentioned but not specified
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Construct discretized payoff vector; compute analytical benchmark and discretization error
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Post-select ancilla outcome |0⟩; measure position register to recover option price amplitudes; optionally use amplitude estimation for improved sampling

speedup_claims.conditions: for expected-value estimation via amplitude estimation
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper discusses amplitude estimation as a possible post-processing improvement, but does not present an experimental benchmark showing the speedup.

speedup_claims.conditions: assuming fault-tolerant gate-based quantum computing and QSP-based simulation
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an algorithmic complexity claim, not an empirical runtime result.

speedup_claims.factor: O(n log n) for QFT subroutine
speedup_claims.conditions: with periodic boundary conditions enabling circulant structure
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states efficient diagonalization is possible via QFT; no direct runtime comparison is reported.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(td||H||_max + log(1/ϵ)/log log(1/ϵ)) for QSP-based sparse Hamiltonian simulation; QFT subroutine O(n log n)
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Not explicitly characterized for the full PDE solver; table compares classical methods such as O(2^n), O(T_steps 2^n), or O(1/ϵ^2) depending on baseline

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: 9 logical qubits in the reported simulation setting (8 spatial qubits + 1 ancilla); QFT-based diagonalization and QSP-based Hamiltonian simulation are the key subroutines.
limiting_factors: No experimental QPU benchmark is reported
No classical runtime comparison on the same instance is provided
The claimed complexity is asymptotic and fault-tolerant
State preparation for the payoff state is nontrivial
Post-selection success probability is only reported as above 60%, which adds overhead

notes: num_qubits=9 is explicitly stated as the total qubit count needed to simulate the dynamics in a fault-tolerant quantum computer (8 spatial qubits + 1 ancilla).
hardware.type is not tied to a specific device; the paper discusses a digital quantum computer/fault-tolerant setting rather than a named QPU, so hardware was inferred as not specified.
circuit_depth is not reported numerically; only algorithmic subroutine complexities (e.g., QFT O(n log n)) are given.
The paper reports an algorithmic simulation study and theoretical complexity claims, but no demonstrated end-to-end quantum advantage over classical methods.
